title: Class-wise Balancing Data Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines a full left-singular-vector matrix U^(i)' ∈ R^{n×n} and computes each sample's leverage score as ||e_{i,j}^T U_k^(i)||_2^2. Every row of a square orthogonal U has squared norm exactly 1, so every stated leverage score is identically 1. Thus the proposed score cannot rank samples or provide the claimed importance-driven sampling. A truncated rank-r matrix U_r, with r<n, would be needed, but no truncation/rank is specified.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1, Eq. (6) and following sampling paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says leverage scores are aggregated into a 'global vector' and normalized into a sampling distribution, but Eq. (6) normalizes p_k^{i,j} only by Σ_{j'=1}^{n_k^i} τ_k^{i,j'}, i.e., separately within each client. This is not a global probability distribution over all client samples as subsequently claimed. Moreover, with the full-U definition, the resulting probability is simply uniform within each client.

No class label, class count, class quota, inverse-frequency term, or class-constrained sampling rule appears in Eqs. (1)–(6) or Algorithm 1. The procedure samples by leverage scores derived solely from features. Such sampling does not mathematically ensure equal per-class counts, class coverage, or class-balanced replay. The central claim that the described mechanism 'enables class-balanced replay' is therefore unsupported by the method as specified.

Eq. (7) applies Softmax(z_i^{old}/τ_old) for old samples and Softmax(z_j^{new}/τ_new) for new samples, apparently normalizing only within the old or new logit subsets. Eq. (9), however, applies one softmax to Concat(f^old/τ_old, f^new/τ_new), which is necessary for old-versus-new class discrimination. These are different objectives, with different normalization and gradients. Eq. (9) also uses separate 1/N_old and 1/N_new prefactors, unlike Eq. (7)'s 1/(N_old+N_new), so it is not the stated L_TTS.

The paper repeatedly calls P_k X_k Q 'encrypted' and 'privacy-preserving.' It is only multiplication by orthogonal matrices, not an encryption scheme, and no cryptographic security definition, threat model, key-management procedure, reconstruction analysis, or feature-inversion/privacy-leakage analysis is provided. The server receives transformed feature matrices and preserves substantial structure (e.g., singular values and Gram-matrix-related information). The asserted privacy guarantee is therefore materially overstated.

Table 4's headers are shifted/mislabeled relative to the values copied from Tables 2–3. For example, under the 3/5/10 split, the column labelled 'CIFAR100 β=0.1' reports Finetune = 15.17±2.2, but Table 2 identifies 15.17±2.2 as CIFAR10 β=0.1. The following values 16.75±2.6 and 17.15±1.3 correspond to CIFAR100 β=0.5 and β=1.0, while 6.06±0.9 corresponds to CIFAR100 β=0.1 but is labelled TinyImageNet β=0.1. This affects every row of the ablation table and invalidates the stated dataset/heterogeneity interpretation.

Both main comparison tables omit all baseline values for TinyImageNet at β=0.1, while FedCBDR reports a value (18.35±1.0 in Table 2) or the column is otherwise incomplete. Nevertheless, Section 5.2 and the abstract frame the work as a comparison across heterogeneous settings and make broad superiority claims. Without baseline results, no comparative conclusion can be drawn for those reported settings.

The abstract and introduction state a '2%–15% Top-1 accuracy improvement compared to several state-of-the-art methods,' while Table 2 contains a direct counterexample: on CIFAR100, 5 tasks, β=1.0, FedCBDR is 52.06±1.5 and LANDER is higher at 52.77±1.4. Section 5.2 later acknowledges this exception, but the headline improvement claim is not qualified to exclude it and therefore misrepresents the table as a general comparative gain.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 and Appendix Table 11, computational-complexity statement
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed client-side iSVD cost O(n_k d^2) omits the cost of multiplying the stated dense P_k ∈ R^{n_k×n_k} by X_k ∈ R^{n_k×d}, which is O(n_k^2 d), as well as generating a dense n_k×n_k random orthogonal matrix (typically O(n_k^3)). Calling P_k X_k Q 'Inverse SVD' does not remove these costs. Thus the stated complexity and the conclusion that the SVD-related overhead is small do not follow from the presented algorithm.

The reported upload sizes contradict the table's stated sample count n=100. For 100 vectors of dimension 512, an FP32 upload is about 0.195 MB (or about 0.391 MB for FP64), not 3.906 MB. The reported 3.906 MB exactly corresponds approximately to 2,000 × 512 FP32 values, despite the table saying 100 samples/client. The 128- and 32-dimensional rows have the same factor-of-20 discrepancy. Therefore the stated communication accounting is numerically inconsistent.

A.1.2 describes Figure 7 as incremental-task accuracy curves and supplies CIFAR/TinyImageNet chart placeholders and a task-accuracy legend. Its caption instead reads: 'Comparison of per-class sample distributions in the replay buffer between FedCBDR and Re-Fed on the CIFAR100 dataset ... 10-task split and 5 clients.' That is a different experiment, which is subsequently described as Figure 8. The figure/caption mismatch prevents interpretation of the claimed incremental-task evidence.

The section states 'As shown in Table 9' and bases claims about per-task final-model performance on that table, but no Table 9 appears anywhere in the supplied paper. It later refers to additional 50/100-client asynchronous experiments but provides no identifiable table or numerical results for them. These claims therefore lack the cited supporting material.

The method is consistently named GDR, but Figure 6 labels the ablations '+GADR' and '+GADR+TTS.' No GADR module is defined. The figure also uses unresolved placeholders such as '![](bird)' and '![](heatmap)' instead of images. Consequently the visual case-study evidence cannot be inspected and is not coherently tied to the proposed method.

The paper attributes Grad-CAM visualizations to citations [59–63], but none is the Grad-CAM paper. References [59]–[62] concern federated learning, feature alignment, deconfounding, and visual-semantic graph classification; [63] is adversarial cross-modal retrieval. The standard Grad-CAM attribution (Selvaraju et al., ICCV 2017) is absent. These citations do not support the claimed visualization method.
